Starting a Frontier Lab in 2026: Compute, Cost and Capital, with a Bangalore Playbook

You want to build a model of your own and the agents that use it. How much compute does that take to train, to experiment and to serve? Where do the GPUs come from, how much money do you need, and who will provide it? This long bonus article works through the whole bill with interactive calculators, then looks closely at what changes if the startup is in Bangalore: India's subsidised GPUs, rupee prices, government funds and a realistic strategy.

1. Three ambitions, three budgets

"Frontier model startup" covers very different companies. The first decision is which race you are in, because it sets the compute bill by orders of magnitude.

2. What frontier costs now

Capital for new labs reached sizes that would have been unthinkable a few years ago. Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, raised about $2 billion at seed in mid-2025. In March 2026, Yann LeCun's AMI Labs raised $1.03 billion at a $3.5 billion pre-money valuation to build world models; in April, Ineffable Intelligence, founded by former DeepMind reinforcement-learning lead David Silver, raised $1.1 billion at a $5.1 billion valuation. A funding tracker puts the median frontier-lab round in 2026 at about $1.07 billion ⚠️.

Seed rounds for new labs

Reported rounds, billions of dollars.

At the other end, DeepSeek showed how efficient a strong model can be. Its V3 technical report lists 2.788 million H800 GPU-hours for the final model (2.664 million for pre-training, 119,000 for context extension and 5,000 for post-training), which it values at $5.576 million at an assumed $2 per GPU-hour. That number is the final run only: it excludes the experiments that came before it, the data, the staff and the cluster itself. Analysts such as Nathan Lambert at Interconnects stress that the real cost of a lab producing such a model is many times higher.

💡 Two different numbers"What did the training run cost?" and "what does it cost to be a lab that can produce that run?" differ by an order of magnitude or more. Investors fund the second number.

3. The training bill, line by line

A useful rule of thumb: training a dense transformer takes about 6 × N × D floating-point operations, where N is the number of parameters (for mixture-of-experts models, the active parameters per token) and D the number of training tokens. Divide by what a GPU actually delivers, its peak speed times the share you achieve (model FLOPs utilisation, MFU), and you get GPU-hours. Both DeepSeek-V3 and Llama 3 405B work out to roughly 35% MFU on this rule, which we use as the default.

Compute budget builder

Our model. Pick a preset or set your own. "Experiments" multiplies the final run to cover ablations, failed runs and smaller test models; "post-training" adds fine-tuning and RL as a share of pre-training.

Two things stand out. First, the final run is often the smaller part of the bill: labs typically spend several times its compute on experiments before committing to it. Second, chip choice and utilisation matter as much as price: moving from 25% to 45% MFU nearly halves the GPU-hours. That is the work of the engineers in kernels and compilers and training frameworks, and the Llama 3 story in Producing Intelligence.

4. Serving the model, and the agents

Training is a one-off; inference is forever. Once a model has users, serving it usually becomes the larger compute bill, and agents make it larger still. Gartner's March 2026 forecast put agentic workloads at 5 to 30 times the tokens per task of a standard chatbot exchange; a Stanford study of coding agents found them consuming about 1,000 times the tokens of code chat, with runs on the same task differing by up to 30 times.

Serving cost calculator

Our model: self-hosted serving on rented GPUs. Throughput per GPU is an assumption that varies hugely with model size, batch size and hardware.

The lesson for founders: price your product per task, not per token, and budget for agent token counts to vary widely. Related reading: the inference engineers and the collapse in token prices.

5. Where to get the GPUs

The four routes from Part 1 apply to a startup, but in a different order. Few new labs build or buy a cluster in year one; most rent, and the question is on what terms.

Startup sourcing options

Tap an option. Prices are 2026 tracker ranges from Part 6; terms vary by deal.

Cloud credit programmes, such as AWS Activate, Google for Startups Cloud, Microsoft for Startups and NVIDIA Inception, can cover early experiments, but amounts and eligibility change often and are small next to a pre-training run. Larger labs have taken investment from cloud and chip companies that is partly delivered as compute; Google's and Amazon's investments in Anthropic are the best-known examples. Such deals bring capacity but also tie the lab to one provider.

7. The Bangalore playbook

For a startup in Bangalore, four things change: access to subsidised national compute, rupee prices for commercial GPUs, government and domestic funding, and the market it should target. Bangalore also brings India's deepest pool of engineering talent at a fraction of US salaries.

7.1 The IndiaAI Mission's compute

The IndiaAI Mission, approved in 2024 with a ₹10,372 crore outlay over five years, had onboarded 38,231 GPUs by March 2026 through a common compute portal, rented to startups, researchers and academic institutions at subsidised rates reported at about ₹65–67 per GPU-hour. Reports in 2026 said startups building foundation models would receive a 100% compute subsidy, against 40% for other AI workloads ⚠️ (anonymous sources).

What an H100-hour costs a Bangalore startup

Rupees per GPU-hour. US prices converted at ₹88/$ (assumed).

7.2 The selected model builders

The government selected startups to build foundation models in phases: Sarvam AI, Soket AI Labs, Gnani.ai and Gan.ai first, and a later report counted 20 proposals, 12 large and 8 small language models. Sarvam is furthest along: it was allocated 4,096 H100 GPUs for six months, with a subsidy of ₹98.68 crore on a compute bill of ₹246.71 crore. Analytics India Magazine reported in October 2026 that the other selected startups had not yet received their GPUs ⚠️, a reminder that allocation and delivery are different things.

7.3 Funding from India

Beyond compute, Indian founders can draw on domestic venture capital, global funds with Indian teams, corporate backers and new government vehicles. The ₹1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) scheme, approved in July 2025, lends long-term at low or zero interest through second-level fund managers; its first cohort in September 2026 backed 22 projects involving ₹4,744 crore of R&D, 14 of them startups. The IVCA's Bharat DeepTech Report counts $11.4 billion of cumulative deep-tech funding from 2015 to mid-2026, with $2.96 billion across 189 deals in 2025 alone. That is a deep pool for a specialised lab, and a shallow one next to a single US frontier round.

7.4 Chips, power and policy

  • Chip access: the US AI diffusion rule, which would have placed India in a middle tier with chip quotas, was rescinded in May 2025; as of mid-2026 no replacement had been published. Indian buyers can import advanced NVIDIA systems, subject to normal export licensing.
  • Data centers: Karnataka approved a Sustainable Data Centre Policy for 2026–2031 targeting 1 GW of IT load and a 10–12% share of India's AI-ready data center capacity, with capital subsidies, power-tariff benefits, electricity duty exemptions and a one-time ₹20 crore payment for very efficient sites, and a push beyond Bengaluru to places such as Mangaluru.
  • Talent: Bangalore's engineering base lowers team costs sharply compared with San Francisco, though experienced large-scale training engineers remain scarce everywhere.

7.5 A realistic strategy

Where a Bangalore lab can winCompeting head-on with US frontier labs on general models would need billions of dollars that Indian funding does not yet supply. The stronger bets are where India has an edge: Indic-language and speech models trained on data US labs lack; domain models for Indian finance, healthcare, law and government; and agents built for Indian enterprises and public services, served cheaply at scale. Use subsidised national compute for training where you can get it, rent commercially for everything else, and keep the option to fine-tune open-weight models rather than pre-train from scratch.

9. Risks

GPU delivery & priceAllocated is not delivered (IndiaAI); B200 rental prices rose 79% in three months on one index.
Depreciation & obsolescenceA new chip generation every year makes owned clusters and long contracts age fast.
Concentration & policyCompute-for-equity deals tie you to one provider; subsidies and export rules can change.

11. Reading the numbers

Training anchors
DeepSeek-V3: 2.788M H800 GPU-hours, $5.576M at an assumed $2/hr (technical report); 37B active parameters, 14.8T tokens. Llama 3 405B: ~30.8M GPU-hours, 15.6T tokens (Meta). The ~35% MFU default is our back-calculation from these.
Funding
Thinking Machines ~$2B seed (mid-2025); AMI Labs $1.03B at $3.5B pre-money (Mar 2026); Ineffable Intelligence $1.1B at $5.1B (Apr 2026); median 2026 frontier round ~$1.07B (tracker ⚠️).
Agents
5–30× tokens per task vs chat (Gartner, Mar 2026); ~1,000× for coding agents vs code chat (Stanford); these measure different things.
India
₹10,372 crore IndiaAI Mission; 38,231 GPUs, 190 projects (Mar 2026); ~₹65–67/GPU-hr subsidised; 100% foundation-model subsidy reported ⚠️; Sarvam 4,096 H100s, ₹98.68 crore of ₹246.71 crore; others' GPUs delayed per AIM ⚠️; Yotta H100 ₹263–386/GPU-hr list; RDI scheme ₹1 lakh crore, first cohort 22 projects; $11.4B deep-tech funding to mid-2026 (IVCA); diffusion rule rescinded May 2025; Karnataka data center policy 2026–31.
